question: What is the Strategy pattern and what problem does it solve?
title: Strategy Pattern Explained
direct_answer: Strategy pattern defines a family of interchangeable algorithms behind a common interface — use it to eliminate if-else chains for behavior that varies by type or context.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can identify the if-else anti-pattern and name the correct fix
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Explaining Strategy as just using interfaces — missing the specific problem it solves
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a before (if-else chain) and after (Strategy interface + implementations) transformation

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
So Strategy pattern is a behavioral pattern that I would explain starting from the problem it solves. 'The problem: you have a method with a big if-else or switch based on some type — if paymentMethod == CREDIT_CARD, do this; else if paymentMethod == UPI, do that; else if paymentMethod == COD, do this other thing. Every time you add a new payment method, you modify this method. That is an OCP violation.'

'The strategy fix: define a PaymentStrategy interface with one method: processPayment(PaymentRequest request). Create one class per algorithm: CreditCardStrategy, UPIStrategy, CODStrategy, each implementing PaymentStrategy with their own logic. The if-else is gone. PaymentService just holds a PaymentStrategy and calls strategy.processPayment(request) — it does not know which strategy it has.'

'The strategy is selected outside — at configuration time or at runtime based on user choice. The context class (PaymentService) does not decide; the caller or a factory does.'

'Real Java example: Comparator is a strategy. Collections.sort(list, comparator) — you inject the sorting algorithm. You can pass any Comparator without modifying sort().'

'Another: Spring Security uses PasswordEncoder as a strategy. You configure BCryptPasswordEncoder or NoOpPasswordEncoder — the auth logic works with any implementation.'

'Key insight: Strategy replaces behavior-switching if-else chains. Every time I see a method doing different things based on a type enum, that is a Strategy pattern opportunity.'

sections.title: Key Points
content: Problem: if-else chains that switch on type to choose behavior — OCP violation
Solution: extract each behavior into a class implementing a common interface
Context class holds a Strategy and delegates to it — does not choose the algorithm
Strategy selected outside context (by caller, factory, or config)
Real Java: Comparator (sorting strategy), PasswordEncoder (auth strategy)
Adding new behavior = new class implementing interface — zero changes to context

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app applying design patterns to a cart service
speakable_v2.hook: Strategy pattern is the antidote to a specific smell — the if-else chain that grows every time you add a new behavior type.

beats.content: Imagine a checkout service: if payment type is CREDIT_CARD do this, else if UPI do that, else if COD do the other thing. Every new payment method means editing this method. That's an OCP violation — the class changes for every extension.

Strategy fixes it: define a PaymentStrategy interface with a single processPayment method. CreditCardStrategy, UPIStrategy, and CODStrategy each implement it with their own logic. PaymentService just holds a PaymentStrategy and calls it — no if-else, no knowledge of which type it got.

content: Context (PaymentService) delegates to strategy — doesn't choose the algorithm
Strategy is injected from outside — by the caller, a factory, or Spring DI
Adding a new payment method = new strategy class, zero changes to PaymentService

speakable_v2.cap: non-obvious: Java's Comparator is the canonical Strategy example. Collections.sort() is the context; the comparison algorithm is the strategy you inject. Lambdas make Strategy a one-liner.

question: How do you implement Strategy pattern for a payment system in Java?
title: Strategy Pattern: Payment System Implementation
direct_answer: Define PaymentStrategy interface, implement CreditCardPayment/UPIPayment/CODPayment classes, and inject the selected strategy into PaymentService at checkout.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can implement the pattern correctly with proper separation of context and strategy
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Putting strategy selection (the if-else) inside the context — defeats the purpose
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show how strategy is injected from outside — via constructor or a factory — keeping PaymentService clean

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
So for a payment system, the Strategy pattern looks like this. I would walk through the implementation:

'Interface: PaymentStrategy with method: PaymentResult process(PaymentRequest request).'

'Concrete strategies: CreditCardPaymentStrategy — validates card, charges via card gateway, returns result. UPIPaymentStrategy — generates UPI payment link, waits for callback, returns status. CODPaymentStrategy — no immediate charge, records payment due, returns PENDING result.'

'Context: PaymentService holds a Map<PaymentMethod, PaymentStrategy> populated at startup. process(orderId, paymentMethod, details) looks up strategy = strategies.get(paymentMethod), calls strategy.process(request), records Payment entity.'

'Strategy selection happens in the controller or service layer before calling PaymentService — based on the user checkout selection. PaymentService itself has no if-else for payment types.'

'Adding a new payment method: create class WalletPaymentStrategy implements PaymentStrategy, register it in the map. PaymentService is untouched. This is OCP — open for extension, closed for modification.'

'In Spring: I would annotate each strategy with @Component. PaymentService gets a Map<String, PaymentStrategy> injected automatically — Spring collects all PaymentStrategy beans by name.'

sections.title: Key Points
content: PaymentStrategy interface: process(PaymentRequest): PaymentResult
One class per payment method — each encapsulates its own gateway logic
PaymentService holds Map<PaymentMethod, PaymentStrategy> — lookup, not if-else
Strategy selection by caller (controller or checkout flow) — not by PaymentService
Spring auto-injection: Map<String, PaymentStrategy> collects all strategy beans
New payment method = new strategy class, zero changes to PaymentService

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app applying design patterns to a cart service
speakable_v2.hook: The payment system example makes Strategy concrete — and showing the before vs after transformation is exactly what interviewers want to see.

beats.content: Define PaymentStrategy with one method: process(PaymentRequest). Write CreditCardPaymentStrategy, UPIPaymentStrategy, CODPaymentStrategy — each handles its own gateway logic.

PaymentService holds a Map from payment method to strategy. At checkout, a lookup replaces the if-else: strategy = strategies.get(paymentMethod), then strategy.process(request). No switch, no conditionals in the service itself.

In Spring, annotate each strategy with @Component. PaymentService gets a Map<String, PaymentStrategy> auto-injected — Spring collects all PaymentStrategy beans by bean name as the map key. Adding WalletPaymentStrategy means one new class — the map grows automatically, PaymentService is untouched.

speakable_v2.cap: sharp edge: The strategy selection still has to happen somewhere. It moves to the caller or a factory — not to the context class. If PaymentService still has an if-else to choose which strategy to use, you've only moved the problem, not solved it.

question: How does Java's Comparator demonstrate the Strategy pattern?
title: Comparator as Strategy Pattern in Java
direct_answer: Comparator is a strategy for comparison — Collections.sort() is the context that accepts any comparison algorithm without knowing its implementation.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can spot Strategy in standard library APIs — not just in textbook examples
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating Comparator as just a utility — missing that it is the canonical Java Strategy pattern example
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show lambda as an anonymous strategy: list.sort((a,b) -> a.getName().compareTo(b.getName()))

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
So Comparator is probably the clearest built-in Strategy pattern example in Java. I would explain it like this:

'Collections.sort(list, comparator) is the context. The sorting algorithm is fixed — it is always a stable sort. But the comparison behavior is the strategy — how to determine if element A comes before element B.'

'Comparator is the strategy interface: int compare(T a, T b). You pass any implementation and sort adapts. Sorting employees by name: new Comparator<Employee>() { public int compare(Employee a, Employee b) { return a.getName().compareTo(b.getName()); } }. Sort by salary: different implementation.'

'With Java 8 lambdas, the strategy becomes even cleaner: list.sort((a, b) -> a.getSalary() - b.getSalary()). A lambda is an anonymous strategy implementation.'

'With Comparator.comparing: list.sort(Comparator.comparing(Employee::getName).thenComparing(Employee::getAge)). This chains strategies — a composed strategy pattern.'

'The key point: sort() (the context) never needs to change. Adding a new sorting criterion is just a new Comparator — not a new sort method.'

'Other built-in Java strategies: Runnable (thread execution strategy), Callable, Predicate (filter strategy in streams), Function (transformation strategy). Most functional interfaces in Java are strategies.'

sections.title: Key Points
content: Comparator = strategy for comparison; sort() = context
New sort order = new Comparator, no change to sort()
Java 8 lambda: anonymous strategy in one line
Comparator.comparing().thenComparing(): composed strategy
Most Java functional interfaces are strategies: Runnable, Predicate, Function
Collections.sort, Arrays.sort, Stream.sorted all accept comparison strategies

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app applying design patterns to a cart service
speakable_v2.hook: Comparator is Strategy in disguise — and it's been in Java since version 1, making it the most used example of the pattern most developers have never noticed.

beats.content: Collections.sort() is the context — the sorting algorithm is fixed. Comparator is the strategy interface — you inject the comparison rule. Sort by name, sort by salary, sort by date: three strategies, one sort method that never changes.

With Java 8 lambdas, the strategy collapses to one line: list.sort((a, b) -> a.getSalary() - b.getSalary()). A lambda is an anonymous strategy implementation. Comparator.comparing(Employee::getName).thenComparing(Employee::getAge) composes multiple strategies in sequence.

speakable_v2.cap: non-obvious: Almost every functional interface in Java is a strategy — Runnable, Predicate, Function, Callable. Strategy pattern is the foundation of the entire functional programming style Java adopted in version 8.
followup_handoff: How does Comparator.reversed() work in terms of strategy composition?

question: How do you use Spring's @Qualifier annotation for Strategy pattern-style selection?
title: Strategy Pattern with Spring @Qualifier
direct_answer: Annotate each strategy implementation with @Component and @Qualifier, then inject the desired strategy using @Autowired and @Qualifier in the context class.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can apply a design pattern using Spring's DI mechanism
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Injecting strategy using new StrategyImpl() inside context — defeats DI and makes testing harder
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show both @Qualifier and Map<String, Strategy> injection — the map approach is more flexible for dynamic selection

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
So Spring makes Strategy pattern very clean through DI. Here are two approaches:

'Approach 1: @Qualifier for fixed strategy. If a service always uses one strategy, annotate: @Component @Qualifier("upi") class UPIPaymentStrategy implements PaymentStrategy. Then inject: @Autowired @Qualifier("upi") PaymentStrategy paymentStrategy. This is clean when the strategy is fixed for the service.'

'Approach 2: Map injection for dynamic selection. All strategies are Spring beans. Inject them all at once: @Autowired Map<String, PaymentStrategy> paymentStrategies. Spring auto-populates the map with bean name as key and the bean as value. At runtime: PaymentStrategy strategy = paymentStrategies.get(selectedMethodName). No if-else anywhere — just a map lookup.'

'The map approach is more flexible for our payment system because the strategy is selected at request time (based on user choice), not at startup. You can add a new strategy just by creating a new @Component class — the map gets populated automatically.'

'For testability: mock the Map in unit tests with specific strategy stubs. Or test each strategy implementation independently — they are just plain Java classes that implement an interface.'

sections.title: Key Points
content: @Qualifier for fixed strategy selection: inject one specific implementation
Map<String, Strategy> injection: Spring auto-populates all strategy beans
Dynamic selection: paymentStrategies.get(methodName) — no if-else
New strategy: new @Component class, auto-registered in the map
Bean naming convention: use consistent names for map key matching
Test isolation: each strategy is a plain Java class, testable independently

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app applying design patterns to a cart service
speakable_v2.hook: Spring makes Strategy pattern nearly effortless — the framework wires all implementations into a map automatically.

beats.content: @Qualifier works for fixed selection: annotate CreditCardPaymentStrategy with @Component and @Qualifier('creditCard'), then inject it where you always want that specific implementation. Straightforward and explicit.

Map injection is more powerful for dynamic selection. Annotate all strategies with @Component. Inject Map<String, PaymentStrategy> into the context service — Spring populates the map with every PaymentStrategy bean, using the bean name as the key. At runtime: strategies.get('upiPaymentStrategy'). Adding a new strategy class automatically registers it in the map with no other changes needed.

speakable_v2.cap: gotcha: Bean names in the map use Spring's default naming convention — typically the class name with the first letter lowercased. If the map lookup returns null, check that your key matches the actual bean name, not what you assumed it would be.

question: How is Strategy pattern different from simple polymorphism via inheritance?
title: Strategy Pattern vs Inheritance Polymorphism
direct_answer: Inheritance polymorphism fixes behavior at class definition time; Strategy injects behavior at runtime, making it composable, swappable, and testable independently.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand when Strategy is better than subclassing
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating them as interchangeable — missing that Strategy enables runtime algorithm swapping
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the composition vs inheritance trade-off and why Strategy is preferred for interchangeable behaviors

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
So both achieve polymorphic behavior but through different mechanisms. Here is the distinction I would draw:

'With inheritance polymorphism: you define a Vehicle base class with calcToll() overridden in Car, Bike, Truck. The toll calculation is baked into the class hierarchy. To add a new toll algorithm, you modify each subclass or add a new override. The behavior is inseparable from the class.'

'With Strategy: you define a TollStrategy interface. The same Car, Bike, Truck classes have no calcToll() — instead, a TollCalculator holds a TollStrategy. You can change the strategy at runtime without changing Car at all. A Car could use WeekendTollStrategy on weekends and PeakHourTollStrategy on Monday morning.'

'The key differences: Runtime swappability — Strategy can change at runtime; inheritance is fixed at compile time. Single responsibility — with Strategy, the class (Car) is responsible for being a car, not for calculating tolls. Testability — you can test TollStrategy implementations independently of Car. Composition — multiple algorithms can be composed; inheritance does not compose cleanly.'

'Bottom line: use inheritance when the behavior is intrinsic to the type identity (a Dog barks because it IS a Dog). Use Strategy when behavior varies independently of the object type.'

sections.title: Key Points
content: Inheritance: behavior is fixed to class, changed by overriding in subclasses
Strategy: behavior is injected, swappable at runtime without changing the class
Strategy enables SRP — class responsible for its domain, not its algorithms
Strategy is independently testable — no host class needed
Strategy composes cleanly (decorator wrapping a strategy)
Rule: behavior intrinsic to type identity → inheritance; behavior varying independently → Strategy

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app applying design patterns to a cart service
speakable_v2.hook: Strategy and polymorphism solve the same problem — but one bakes behavior into the class at compile time and the other injects it at runtime.

beats.content: With inheritance polymorphism, the algorithm is tied to the class. A Car subclass overrides calcToll() and that's fixed. If toll rules change on weekends, you'd need to subclass Car again or add conditional logic inside calcToll().

With Strategy, the same Car class holds a TollStrategy reference. You can swap in WeekendTollStrategy at runtime without touching Car. The algorithm changes independently of the object. That's composition over inheritance — the GoF's own recommendation.

speakable_v2.cap: sharp edge: Use inheritance when behavior is intrinsic to type identity — a Dog barks because it IS a Dog. Use Strategy when behavior varies independently of the type — a Car uses different toll rules depending on day and time, not on what kind of car it is.
